screens.title: Deep Dive into SELinux Policy Management
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will treat SELinux as a system-wide guardrail for processes and files. You will learn the mental model of Mandatory Access Control versus Discretionary Access Control, how SELinux labels resources with contexts, and how to analyze and resolve denials without disabling protection. We’ll walk through practical commands you will use every day: checking mode with the enforcement command, inspecting contexts with contextual listing, and reviewing AVC denials from the audit log. Most importantly, you will practice generating and installing narrow policy modules so the system permits only what you explicitly allow. The goal is to give you a repeatable workflow: reproduce the denial, collect audit entries, generate a candidate policy, compile it, and load it safely. This matters because broad or ad-hoc fixes weaken security; precise policy changes preserve the system’s defenses while enabling required functionality. As you proceed, notice the difference between labels that describe ownership and labels that describe allowed interactions. By the end of the chapter you will be able to resolve application denials with confidence and keep SELinux in enforcing mode in production. Consider this: what minimal permission would let your service function while keeping risk low?

Deep Dive into SELinux Policy Management

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives outline the concrete skills you will be able to demonstrate after completing the chapter. First, you will be able to explain the fundamental difference between Discretionary Access Control and Mandatory Access Control and argue why SELinux as MAC hardens a system against privilege escalation. Second, you will manage SELinux modes and labels for files, directories, and processes, applying tools like getenforce, setenforce, ls -Z, ps -Z, semanage, and restorecon. Third, you will diagnose Access Vector Cache denials by reading audit. log entries and using ausearch and sealert to extract actionable information. Finally, you will generate, compile, and install custom SELinux policy modules using audit2allow, checkmodule, semodule_package, and semodule so services can perform required actions without turning SELinux off. Each objective is a practical capability; for example, after this chapter you can convert an AVC denial into a minimal policy rule that allows a web server to write to a custom log directory while keeping the rest of the system protected. You will also practice the discipline of testing in permissive mode before enabling changes in enforcing mode.

screens.title: MAC vs DAC — Why SELinux is different
screens.narratorSegment: Start by anchoring the difference between DAC and MAC. Discretionary Access Control ties permissions to the resource owner; the owner can change access lists and decide who may read or write. By contrast, Mandatory Access Control implements system-wide rules that users and even root cannot override. SELinux is a MAC implementation: it labels subjects and objects with contexts and enforces rules based on those labels. A concrete example: under DAC a process running as root could freely open files if Unix permissions allow, and root can change owner or mode. Under SELinux MAC, even a root-owned process in an unprivileged domain can be denied actions if its type policy does not permit them. The practical significance for architects is clear: SELinux reduces the blast radius of a compromised process by constraining what it can do, even if it obtains elevated user privileges. A common misconception is that SELinux replaces Unix permissions; it does not. Instead, it layers more granular checks. When designing systems, treat DAC and MAC as complementary. Ask yourself: if a service is compromised, what are the independent controls you can rely on to limit access?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › MAC vs DAC
Core Concept

MAC vs DAC

Understand why SELinux’s Mandatory Access Control complements ordinary Unix permissions and how that limits an attacker's reach.

Discretionary Access Control (DAC)
Owner-based permissions, changeable by users or root. Useful but insufficient against compromised services.
Mandatory Access Control (MAC)
System-enforced, label-driven policy that cannot be bypassed by users. SELinux is a MAC providing type enforcement.
Misconception
SELinux does not replace file permissions; it layers on top and enforces additional constraints based on types and contexts.
Scenario
A web server running as a service process obtains root via exploit. UNIX permissions may allow file access, but SELinux can stop the compromised process from reading or writing files outside its allowed types, limiting damage.
Check your understanding
  • Does SELinux replace owner-based permissions? No — it complements them.
  • Can root override SELinux policy by normal commands? No — policy is enforced at kernel level.

screens.title: SELinux Modes — Enforcing, Permissive, Disabled
screens.narratorSegment: SELinux supports three operational modes: enforcing, permissive, and disabled. Enforcing applies policy decisions and blocks unauthorized actions while logging AVC denials. Permissive records the denials but does not block the actions, which makes it invaluable when diagnosing why an application fails under SELinux. Disabled turns off SELinux entirely, removing MAC protections and is discouraged for production systems. A common troubleshooting workflow begins with enforcing in production, but when diagnosing a new failure you can temporarily move to permissive to collect denials without breaking functionality. Use getenforce to query the current mode and setenforce to switch modes temporarily; persistent changes belong in /etc/selinux/config. A common mistake is to leave a system in permissive mode once the issue appears resolved: permissive can hide policy gaps. Instead, gather sufficient audit data in permissive, convert denials into a minimal policy module or correct file contexts, then return to enforcing and re-verify. For example, if a web server cannot write to /opt/myapp/logs, setenforce Permissive, reproduce the write attempt to collect AVC entries, and use those entries to create an allow rule before returning to enforcing mode.

keyIdea.text: Use permissive for diagnosis, enforce for production, and avoid disabled except as last resort; persist changes only via config edits and test before returning to enforcing.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › SELinux Modes
Definition

Enforcing, Permissive, Disabled

Learn the safe workflow for mode changes and why permissive is for diagnostics only.

Enforcing
Blocks unauthorized actions and writes AVC denials to the audit log.
Permissive
Allows actions but logs the denials for analysis.
Disabled
Turns SELinux off. Avoid in production; it removes mandatory controls.
Common commands
getenforce
setenforce Permissive
setenforce Enforcing
# edit /etc/selinux/config for persistent mode
Guided example
If a web server write fails, switch to permissive, reproduce the write to generate AVC entries, then use those entries to build a minimal allow rule and return to enforcing once validated.

screens.title: SELinux Contexts and Type Enforcement
screens.narratorSegment: At the core of SELinux is the context attached to every file, process, and port. Contexts use four fields: user, role, type, and level. In practical administration the most important field is type because Type Enforcement defines which types may interact. For example, a directory labeled system_u:object_r:httpd_sys_content_t:s0 is type httpd_sys_content_t and the httpd process runs in a domain type such as httpd_t. The policy contains rules that allow or deny interactions between httpd_t and httpd_sys_content_t. You can view file contexts using the contextual listing command and see process contexts with a process listing that includes SELinux labels. If a file is moved from another filesystem or created by a user, its context can be wrong for the service that must access it. Restoring the default context is done with restorecon, and persistent context mappings are declared with semanage fcontext. A frequent error is to change Unix ownership or mode to try to fix a denial; that often fails because SELinux's type is still mismatched. Always check both DAC and MAC when troubleshooting. As a concrete example, after moving web assets into /opt, run semanage fcontext to map the path to httpd_sys_content_t, then restorecon to apply the label so the web server can serve the content under enforcing mode.

keyIdea.text: Type within the context drives SELinux decisions. Inspect with ls -Z and ps -Z, map paths with semanage fcontext, and apply labels with restorecon.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › SELinux Contexts
Definition

Contexts & Type Enforcement

A context labels resources with user:role:type:level. The type field enforces what can interact with what.

Inspecting contexts
Use ls -Z for files and ps -Z for processes to reveal their SELinux contexts.
Correcting labels
Declare persistent mappings with semanage fcontext and apply them with restorecon -Rv.
Example context
system_u:object_r:httpd_sys_content_t:s0 system_u:system_r:httpd_t:s0
The httpd process type httpd_t is checked against the file type httpd_sys_content_t by the policy.
Common mistake
Changing ownership or Unix permissions alone may not fix SELinux denials if the type is incorrect. Always verify and correct the context.

screens.title: Mapping file contexts persistently
screens.narratorSegment: When files are created in non-standard locations, the system default labels may not be appropriate. Declaring a persistent mapping tells SELinux what type to apply whenever restorecon runs or when a file is relabeled. Use semanage fcontext -a -t " " to add a mapping and then restorecon -Rv to label existing files. An example workflow: you deploy application logs at /opt/myapp/logs. Add a mapping semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_log_t "/opt/myapp/logs(/.*)?" and then restorecon -Rv /opt/myapp/logs. This ensures future relabel operations keep the httpd_log_t type. A common misconception is that semanage applies the label immediately; it only stores the mapping. restorecon applies stored mappings to the filesystem. If you omit semanage and only run restorecon after a move, labels may revert on relabel or boot. For persistent deployments and automation, include semanage declarations in your configuration scripts so contexts survive package upgrades and system relabels. Finally, verify with ls -Z to confirm the applied type matches what your service expects. Mapping file contexts persistently means semanage fcontext declares a mapping; restorecon applies it. use both to ensure labels persist across relabels and reboots.. In practical terms, use semanage fcontext and restorecon to keep labels stable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Persistent Contexts
Process Flow

Declare and apply persistent file contexts

Step 1 — Declare mapping
semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_log_t "/opt/myapp/logs(/.*)?"
This stores the mapping in the SELinux policy store.
Step 2 — Apply mapping
restorecon -Rv /opt/myapp/logs
This applies stored mappings to existing files and directories.
Verify
Confirm with ls -Z /opt/myapp/logs and ensure the type matches what your service expects.

screens.title: Analyzing AVC Denials in the Audit Log
screens.narratorSegment: When SELinux blocks an action, the kernel writes an Access Vector Cache denial into the audit log. These AVC messages contain subject context, target context, class, and the requested permissions. The canonical triage commands are ausearch and sealert. Use ausearch -m AVC -ts today to view recent denials, or filter by process name to focus on the service you are troubleshooting. sealert -a /var/log/audit/audit. log provides a companion, human-readable summary that often suggests corrective steps. For a concrete example, if an httpd process is denied write access to /opt/myapp/logs, an AVC entry will show scontext=httpd_t and tcontext=some_type and class=file with a { write } permission. From that, you can decide whether to relabel the directory to a permitted type or create a narrow policy to allow httpd_t the specific file class operations. A common misconception is to immediately disable SELinux when seeing many AVCs; instead, triage patterns to determine which are expected, which are mislabels, and which require policy changes. Start in permissive to collect complete data if you need more entries, and use timestamps and process filters to isolate the relevant AVCs before constructing a policy.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › AVC Denials
Process Flow

Collect AVCs and interpret fields

Focus on subject context, target context, class, and the requested permission to determine the appropriate fix.

Useful commands
ausearch -m AVC -ts today
ausearch -c httpd -m AVC -ts today
sealert -a /var/log/audit/audit.log
Interpretation
Identify scontext (subject), tcontext (target), class (object type), and the permission set; use that to choose relabel or policy allow.
Example AVC entry breakdown
type=AVC msg=...: avc: denied { write } for pid=2345 comm="httpd" scontext=system_u:system_r:httpd_t:s0 tcontext=system_u:object_r:etc_t:s0 tclass=file
This shows httpd_t attempted a file write to a file labeled etc_t. Decide whether relabel or a minimal policy is appropriate.
Common mistake
Responding to many AVCs by disabling SELinux loses the protection SELinux provides. Triage and address root causes with targeted fixes.

screens.title: Generating a policy: audit2allow and .te files
screens.narratorSegment: Once you have AVC entries, the next step is to generate a candidate policy. audit2allow examines audit log denials and translates them into Type Enforcement rules. A common command is audit2allow -a /var/log/audit/audit. log -M myapp_httpd_log which produces a. te file and a packaged module named myapp_httpd_log. pp. Alternatively, use ausearch to extract denials for a specific process and pipe to audit2allow. The generated. te contains a module header, require blocks with the types and classes used, and allow rules like allow httpd_t var_log_t:file { append read write };. Treat audit2allow output as a draft: audit entries may include multiple simultaneous denials and audit2allow can recommend broader permissions than you intend. Always read the. te and refine it to adhere to least privilege. For example, prefer restricting file classes to only append and write for a log file instead of allowing broad directory write access. Generate the. te in a controlled environment, review the require block for only expected types, and prepare to compile it into a. pp for loading into the kernel. Generating a policy: audit2allow and .te files means use audit2allow to convert avcs into a .te file, then review and narrow the suggested rules before compiling and installing.. In practical terms, parse denials and produce a type enforcement file. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › audit2allow
Code Walkthrough

Generate a .te from AVC denials

Use audit2allow to translate collected denials into a starter Type Enforcement file, then review and tighten the rules.

Typical command
audit2allow -a /var/log/audit/audit.log -M myapp_httpd_log
Inspect .te
Open the generated myapp_httpd_log.te and verify the require block and allow statements are narrowly scoped.
Example .te snippet
module mycustom_httpd 1.0;

require {
  type httpd_t;
  type var_log_t;
  class file { append read write };
}

#============= httpd_t ==============
allow httpd_t var_log_t:file { append read write };
Review the file carefully and remove any allow statements that are broader than required.
Misconception
Do not install generated modules unmodified into production. Audit-generated suggestions are a starting point that you must refine for least privilege.

screens.title: Compile and install policy modules
screens.narratorSegment: After preparing and reviewing a Type Enforcement file, compile it into a module and install it. The standard steps are checkmodule to produce a module object, semodule_package to make a package file, and semodule to install it. For example: checkmodule -M -m -o mycustom_httpd. mod mycustom_httpd. te then semodule_package -o mycustom_httpd. pp -m mycustom_httpd. mod and finally semodule -i mycustom_httpd. pp. After installation, test the service behavior and recheck audit logs. If you are unsure, install the module in permissive mode and monitor. If the module fixes the issue without opening unrelated permissions, move to enforcing and verify again. Remember that semodule installations persist across reboots. To remove a module, use semodule -r. Testing is critical: an overly broad module defeats SELinux’s purpose. You can also let sealert suggest a module which you still inspect before installing. Always keep module source (. te) in version control so you can audit changes and roll back problematic modules quickly. Compile and install policy modules means compile with checkmodule, package with semodule_package, and install with semodule -i. test thoroughly and keep .te in version control.. Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Compile & Install
Process

Compile and deploy a policy module

Use checkmodule, semodule_package, and semodule to build and install a policy. Keep policy sources under version control.

Commands
checkmodule -M -m -o mycustom_httpd.mod mycustom_httpd.te
semanage_package -o mycustom_httpd.pp -m mycustom_httpd.mod  # alternative name
semodule_package -o mycustom_httpd.pp -m mycustom_httpd.mod
semodule -i mycustom_httpd.pp
Verification
After install, replicate the action that originally caused the AVC and ensure no further denials, then check audit.log.
Rollback
Remove a module with semodule -r mycustom_httpd and keep .te files under source control to track changes.
Pro tip
Test modules in permissive first and prefer narrower file class permissions like append or write instead of broad directory writes.

screens.title: Relabel vs Allow: When to change contexts and when to write policy
screens.narratorSegment: When confronted with an AVC denial, you must decide whether the appropriate fix is to relabel the file or to grant the process additional permissions via policy. If the resource is legitimately part of a service’s normal filesystem role, relabeling is often correct: define the persistent fcontext and restorecon so the file has the expected type. For example, configuration files belonging to myapp should carry myapp_conf_t so myapp_t can read them. Conversely, if the service legitimately needs a new capability not covered by existing types — for instance, writing to a non-standard log location — creating a minimal policy module that allows specific file operations for the process type may be appropriate. A key heuristic: relabel when the resource logically belongs to the service; write policy when the resource is separate but must be accessed. Avoid blanket allow rules that open directories or wide classes. Always test in permissive and validate that your change addresses the exact denial messages without introducing unrelated permissions. This decision process is central to maintaining least privilege while keeping applications functioning. Relabel vs Allow: When to change contexts and when to write policy means relabel when the resource should be part of the service’s domain; add policy when access to a separate resource is legitimately required. prefer narrow rules.. In practical terms, choosing between semanage/restorecon and building a custom module. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Relabel vs Policy
Comparison

When to relabel and when to allow

Use relabel for resources that logically belong to the service; use policy when access is required to separate resources.

Relabeling
Use semanage fcontext and restorecon for paths that should carry an existing type compatible with service policy.
Policy module
Use audit2allow and create a focused module when the action is legitimate but the resource should not be relabeled.
Scenario examples
  • Relabel: application config files placed under /etc/myapp — map to myapp_conf_t.
  • Policy: third-party storage at /mnt/shared/logs where only a few write ops are needed — craft a module to allow specific file write ops.
Check your understanding
If the resource logically belongs to the application, relabeling is usually the right remedy. Otherwise prefer policy with minimal allow statements.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Lab: httpd logs
Hands-on Activity

Allow httpd to write to /opt/myapp/logs

Step 1 — Reproduce
Create the path and trigger a write to generate AVCs.
sudo mkdir -p /opt/myapp/logs
sudo touch /opt/myapp/logs/access.log
sudo -u apache touch /opt/myapp/logs/test_write.log
Step 2 — Collect
Use ausearch to extract relevant AVC entries.
ausearch -c httpd -m AVC -ts today
Step 3 — Generate
Create a draft policy with audit2allow and review it carefully.
audit2allow -a /var/log/audit/audit.log -M myapp_httpd_log
Step 4 — Compile & Install
Build the package and install it into the running policy.
checkmodule -M -m -o myapp_httpd.mod myapp_httpd.te
semodule_package -o myapp_httpd.pp -m myapp_httpd.mod
semodule -i myapp_httpd.pp
Step 5 — Verify
Re-run the write attempt and validate no AVCs remain, then setenforce 1 to re-enable enforcing behavior.
Optional — Relabel
If relabeling is preferred, declare a mapping and apply it.
semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_log_t "/opt/myapp/logs(/.*)?"
restorecon -Rv /opt/myapp/logs

screens.title: Policy design and common mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: Good policy design follows the principle of least privilege. That means granting the minimum file classes and operations required for the service to function. Keep policy source files (. te) in version control, annotate why a rule exists, and include tests that reproduce the original AVC. Common mistakes include installing audit2allow suggestions without review, granting directory-level write to a web server when only append is needed for log files, and leaving systems in permissive mode indefinitely. Also avoid using disabled mode as a troubleshooting shortcut. Instead, collect the necessary audit entries, craft a narrow module or relabel as appropriate, and then move back to enforcing. Use semodule -l to list installed modules and semodule -r to remove suspect modules. Finally, document changes for operations and auditing. When working in teams, require peer review of policy changes so unexpected permissions do not creep in. The combination of review, testing, and conservative rules keeps SELinux effective and maintainable as part of the system security architecture. Policy design and common mistakes means adopt least privilege, review audit2allow output, test modules, store policy sources in version control, and avoid permissive as a permanent state.. In practical terms, least privilege, version control, and avoiding broad fixes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Policy Design
Best Practices

Least privilege and process

Least privilege
Grant specific file classes like append or write, not broad directory access.
Version control
Store .te sources and document policy rationale to support audits and rollbacks.
Common mistakes and fixes
  • Installing autogenerated modules without review — always inspect the .te first.
  • Using permissive as permanent state — collect data in permissive, then implement precise fixes and return to enforcing.
  • Granting broad permissions out of convenience — prefer targeted allow statements and relabeling where appropriate.
Operational checks
Use semodule -l to list modules, semodule -r to remove, and retest your application behavior after changes.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: These are the compact ideas to carry forward. First, Mandatory Access Control enforces system policies independent of ownership, and SELinux provides Type Enforcement using contexts to control interactions. Second, files and processes carry contexts with a four-field form; the type field controls permitted interactions and is central to SELinux decisions. Third, AVC denials tell you which subject attempted which action on which object; use ausearch and sealert to gather and interpret them. Fourth, generate candidate policies with audit2allow, but always review and narrow them to respect least privilege. Fifth, persist context mappings with semanage fcontext and apply them with restorecon, and compile policies with checkmodule and semodule_package before installing with semodule. Keep policy sources in version control and test in permissive then enforcing so you maintain protection without breaking functionality. These key concepts form the basis of SELinux administration for reliable, secure production systems.

MAC vs DAC
MAC enforces system policies independent of file ownership; SELinux implements MAC.
SELinux Context
Labels use user:role:type:level; the type field drives Type Enforcement rules.
AVC Denial
Audit messages show scontext, tcontext, class, and requested permissions — the inputs for triage.
Policy Modules
Generate .te with audit2allow, compile and package, then install with semodule -i.
Context Management
Use semanage fcontext and restorecon to persist and apply labels.
Booleans & Controls
Booleans can toggle policy behavior, but changing them should be documented and limited.
Summary takeaway

SELinux enforces type-based rules. Triage via audit logs, prefer relabeling when logical, and craft narrow policy modules when needed. Test, document, and control changes.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will treat SELinux as a system-wide guardrail for processes and files. You will learn the mental model of Mandatory Access Control versus Discretionary Access Control, how SELinux labels resources with contexts, and how to analyze and resolve denials without disabling protection. We’ll walk through practical commands you will use every day: checking mode with the enforcement command, inspecting contexts with contextual listing, and reviewing AVC denials from the audit log. Most importantly, you will practice generating and installing narrow policy modules so the system permits only what you explicitly allow. The goal is to give you a repeatable workflow: reproduce the denial, collect audit entries, generate a candidate policy, compile it, and load it safely. This matters because broad or ad-hoc fixes weaken security; precise policy changes preserve the system’s defenses while enabling required functionality. As you proceed, notice the difference between labels that describe ownership and labels that describe allowed interactions. By the end of the chapter you will be able to resolve application denials with confidence and keep SELinux in enforcing mode in production. Consider this: what minimal permission would let your service function while keeping risk low?

These objectives outline the concrete skills you will be able to demonstrate after completing the chapter. First, you will be able to explain the fundamental difference between Discretionary Access Control and Mandatory Access Control and argue why SELinux as MAC hardens a system against privilege escalation. Second, you will manage SELinux modes and labels for files, directories, and processes, applying tools like getenforce, setenforce, ls -Z, ps -Z, semanage, and restorecon. Third, you will diagnose Access Vector Cache denials by reading audit. log entries and using ausearch and sealert to extract actionable information. Finally, you will generate, compile, and install custom SELinux policy modules using audit2allow, checkmodule, semodule_package, and semodule so services can perform required actions without turning SELinux off. Each objective is a practical capability; for example, after this chapter you can convert an AVC denial into a minimal policy rule that allows a web server to write to a custom log directory while keeping the rest of the system protected. You will also practice the discipline of testing in permissive mode before enabling changes in enforcing mode.

This second objectives slide connects skills directly to tasks you will perform. You will practice switching modes safely: use permissive to collect denying events and enforcing for production protection. You will inspect contexts and correct mislabels with semanage fcontext and restorecon so services can access their configuration and data. You will parse AVC denials to understand exactly which subject, object, and class caused the block, and you will use audit2allow to create a Type Enforcement file that expresses the minimal rule needed. You will compile that file into a policy package and install it, verifying behavior before returning to enforcing mode. Why does this matter? In production you cannot rely on disabling SELinux; the architect’s responsibility is to keep applications functional without introducing broad allowances. As a practical example, you will enable a web server to write to /opt/myapp/logs by labeling the directory correctly and, if necessary, installing a narrowly scoped module. Each objective is task-oriented so you can demonstrate competency during an audit or certification lab.

Start by anchoring the difference between DAC and MAC. Discretionary Access Control ties permissions to the resource owner; the owner can change access lists and decide who may read or write. By contrast, Mandatory Access Control implements system-wide rules that users and even root cannot override. SELinux is a MAC implementation: it labels subjects and objects with contexts and enforces rules based on those labels. A concrete example: under DAC a process running as root could freely open files if Unix permissions allow, and root can change owner or mode. Under SELinux MAC, even a root-owned process in an unprivileged domain can be denied actions if its type policy does not permit them. The practical significance for architects is clear: SELinux reduces the blast radius of a compromised process by constraining what it can do, even if it obtains elevated user privileges. A common misconception is that SELinux replaces Unix permissions; it does not. Instead, it layers more granular checks. When designing systems, treat DAC and MAC as complementary. Ask yourself: if a service is compromised, what are the independent controls you can rely on to limit access?

SELinux supports three operational modes: enforcing, permissive, and disabled. Enforcing applies policy decisions and blocks unauthorized actions while logging AVC denials. Permissive records the denials but does not block the actions, which makes it invaluable when diagnosing why an application fails under SELinux. Disabled turns off SELinux entirely, removing MAC protections and is discouraged for production systems. A common troubleshooting workflow begins with enforcing in production, but when diagnosing a new failure you can temporarily move to permissive to collect denials without breaking functionality. Use getenforce to query the current mode and setenforce to switch modes temporarily; persistent changes belong in /etc/selinux/config. A common mistake is to leave a system in permissive mode once the issue appears resolved: permissive can hide policy gaps. Instead, gather sufficient audit data in permissive, convert denials into a minimal policy module or correct file contexts, then return to enforcing and re-verify. For example, if a web server cannot write to /opt/myapp/logs, setenforce Permissive, reproduce the write attempt to collect AVC entries, and use those entries to create an allow rule before returning to enforcing mode.

At the core of SELinux is the context attached to every file, process, and port. Contexts use four fields: user, role, type, and level. In practical administration the most important field is type because Type Enforcement defines which types may interact. For example, a directory labeled system_u:object_r:httpd_sys_content_t:s0 is type httpd_sys_content_t and the httpd process runs in a domain type such as httpd_t. The policy contains rules that allow or deny interactions between httpd_t and httpd_sys_content_t. You can view file contexts using the contextual listing command and see process contexts with a process listing that includes SELinux labels. If a file is moved from another filesystem or created by a user, its context can be wrong for the service that must access it. Restoring the default context is done with restorecon, and persistent context mappings are declared with semanage fcontext. A frequent error is to change Unix ownership or mode to try to fix a denial; that often fails because SELinux's type is still mismatched. Always check both DAC and MAC when troubleshooting. As a concrete example, after moving web assets into /opt, run semanage fcontext to map the path to httpd_sys_content_t, then restorecon to apply the label so the web server can serve the content under enforcing mode.

When files are created in non-standard locations, the system default labels may not be appropriate. Declaring a persistent mapping tells SELinux what type to apply whenever restorecon runs or when a file is relabeled. Use semanage fcontext -a -t " " to add a mapping and then restorecon -Rv to label existing files. An example workflow: you deploy application logs at /opt/myapp/logs. Add a mapping semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_log_t "/opt/myapp/logs(/.*)?" and then restorecon -Rv /opt/myapp/logs. This ensures future relabel operations keep the httpd_log_t type. A common misconception is that semanage applies the label immediately; it only stores the mapping. restorecon applies stored mappings to the filesystem. If you omit semanage and only run restorecon after a move, labels may revert on relabel or boot. For persistent deployments and automation, include semanage declarations in your configuration scripts so contexts survive package upgrades and system relabels. Finally, verify with ls -Z to confirm the applied type matches what your service expects. Mapping file contexts persistently means semanage fcontext declares a mapping; restorecon applies it. use both to ensure labels persist across relabels and reboots.. In practical terms, use semanage fcontext and restorecon to keep labels stable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When SELinux blocks an action, the kernel writes an Access Vector Cache denial into the audit log. These AVC messages contain subject context, target context, class, and the requested permissions. The canonical triage commands are ausearch and sealert. Use ausearch -m AVC -ts today to view recent denials, or filter by process name to focus on the service you are troubleshooting. sealert -a /var/log/audit/audit. log provides a companion, human-readable summary that often suggests corrective steps. For a concrete example, if an httpd process is denied write access to /opt/myapp/logs, an AVC entry will show scontext=httpd_t and tcontext=some_type and class=file with a { write } permission. From that, you can decide whether to relabel the directory to a permitted type or create a narrow policy to allow httpd_t the specific file class operations. A common misconception is to immediately disable SELinux when seeing many AVCs; instead, triage patterns to determine which are expected, which are mislabels, and which require policy changes. Start in permissive to collect complete data if you need more entries, and use timestamps and process filters to isolate the relevant AVCs before constructing a policy.

Once you have AVC entries, the next step is to generate a candidate policy. audit2allow examines audit log denials and translates them into Type Enforcement rules. After preparing and reviewing a Type Enforcement file, compile it into a module and install it. When confronted with an AVC denial, you must decide whether the appropriate fix is to relabel the file or to grant the process additional permissions via policy. If the resource is legitimately part of a service’s normal filesystem role, relabeling is often correct: define the persistent fcontext and restorecon so the file has the expected type. For example, configuration files belonging to myapp should carry myapp_conf_t so myapp_t can read them. Conversely, if the service legitimately needs a new capability not covered by existing types — for instance, writing to a non-standard log location — creating a minimal policy module that allows specific file operations for the process type may be appropriate. A key heuristic: relabel when the resource logically belongs to the service; write policy when the resource is separate but must be accessed. Avoid blanket allow rules that open directories or wide classes. Always test in permissive and validate that your change addresses the exact denial messages without introducing unrelated permissions. This decision process is central to maintaining least privilege while keeping applications functioning. Good policy design follows the principle of least privilege. That means granting the minimum file classes and operations required for the service to function. Keep policy source files (. te) in version control, annotate why a rule exists, and include tests that reproduce the original AVC. Common mistakes include installing audit2allow suggestions without review, granting directory-level write to a web server when only append is needed for log files, and leaving systems in permissive mode indefinitely. Also avoid using disabled mode as a troubleshooting shortcut. Instead, collect the necessary audit entries, craft a narrow module or relabel as appropriate, and then move back to enforcing. Use semodule -l to list installed modules and semodule -r to remove suspect modules. Finally, document changes for operations and auditing. These are the compact ideas to carry forward. First, Mandatory Access Control enforces system policies independent of ownership, and SELinux provides Type Enforcement using contexts to control interactions. Second, files and processes carry contexts with a four-field form; the type field controls permitted interactions and is central to SELinux decisions. Third, AVC denials tell you which subject attempted which action on which object; use ausearch and sealert to gather and interpret them. Fourth, generate candidate policies with audit2allow, but always review and narrow them to respect least privilege. Fifth, persist context mappings with semanage fcontext and apply them with restorecon, and compile policies with checkmodule and semodule_package before installing with semodule. Keep policy sources in version control and test in permissive then enforcing so you maintain protection without breaking functionality. These key concepts form the basis of SELinux administration for reliable, secure production systems.

Keep three operating principles in mind: first, always prefer precise fixes over disabling SELinux; the whole point of Type Enforcement is to reduce attack surface without impeding legitimate behavior. Second, treat audit logs as the truth for what SELinux observed; use ausearch and sealert to extract meaningful rules rather than guessing. Third, adopt a disciplined change process: generate module drafts, refine them, keep. te under version control, test in permissive, and then move to enforcing. These practices ensure SELinux remains an effective layer of defense while allowing services to operate reliably.
